name: Invariant
description: My startup. Point it at an app and it scans three ways: a Playwright pass over the public URL, an offline analysis of a recorded login session, and a call graph of the codebase with 8 graph-level analyses. Findings stream into a dashboard and land on GitHub PRs as comments. 30 founder conversations so far, 12 founders validated it.

deepdive.tagline: Reads your code and your running app together, so a finding shows up with both halves of the story.
deepdive.overview: I'm building Invariant solo. It started as a static analyzer and grew into three scanners feeding one dashboard: a public-URL scan, an authenticated session recorder, and a codebase call graph. The CLI is Rust, the scan engine is Python, the dashboard is Next.js.
deepdive.why: Every team I worked with ran a pile of tools that didn't talk to each other, and none of them knew how the code related to the deployed app. I wanted one place where a slow endpoint, the query behind it and the line that wrote it show up together.

components.name: Web scanner
components.description: Checks a public URL across 7 categories, including stack fingerprinting from live traffic, and produces a report you can share.

components.name: Call graph engine
components.description: 9 node types and 10 edge types. On top of the graph it runs 8 analyses, like duplicate fetches, unbounded fan-out, circular dependencies and endpoints with no auth. Progress streams over SSE.

components.name: Rust CLI
components.description: scan, push, a terminal report, device-flow login, and record/analyze: capture an authenticated browser session and analyze it offline.

components.name: Graph view
components.description: Four views of the same graph: topology, modules, a request trace and blast radius. Replaced my first D3 version in August.

components.name: clipy
components.description: The session-replay part, pulled out as a standalone open-source tool.

metrics: 9 node types · 10 edge types · 8 graph analyses
Self-scan: 157 files, 126 findings in 1.8 s
30 founder conversations · 15 demos
Live: invar-v4.vercel.app

name: HippoVoice
description: Long-term memory for voice companions. Memories fade unless they matter or get recalled, and retrieval walks an association graph instead of only matching vectors. On LoCoMo it ties a Mem0-style baseline on recall (29.47% vs 29.11%) and pulls in a third as much irrelevant context. Runs end to end behind Qwen2.5-Omni.

deepdive.tagline: Memory that forgets the way people do. Breakfast three weeks ago fades; the thing you mentioned once and cared about sticks.
deepdive.overview: HippoVoice started as a demo I built for Rumik and turned into a proper research project. It combines Ebbinghaus-style decay, emotion-weighted salience and HippoRAG-style graph retrieval. I reimplemented Mem0, A-MEM and a Zep-style baseline on the same harness, because published LoCoMo numbers use different models and lenient LLM judges, and I wanted a comparison I could trust.
deepdive.why: Plain RAG keeps every turn forever and retrieves by similarity. That's fine on a small benchmark and gets noisier the longer a companion runs. I wanted memory that stays clean as it grows, and a test setup honest enough to tell me if it does.

components.name: Decay and salience
components.description: Ebbinghaus forgetting curves with a decay multiplier per emotion. Salience drops every turn unless something boosts it.

components.name: Graph retrieval
components.description: Vector and BM25 seeds, then a one-hop walk over the association graph, scored by relevance blended with salience.

components.name: Fair baselines
components.description: Mem0-style, A-MEM-style and Zep-style systems run on identical infrastructure with LoCoMo's published token-F1 scorer.

components.name: Voice pipeline
components.description: The same memory behind an audio-to-audio model. A fact said in one spoken turn is recalled correctly after an unrelated turn in between.

metrics: LoCoMo, 1,540 questions: 29.47% vs 29.11% for Mem0-style at matched settings. A tie, and I report it as one
Contamination test: 10% irrelevant context retrieved vs 30% for Mem0-style and plain RAG
Audio-to-audio: 25.81% avg F1 on a 40-question run with zero errors
My early lead over Mem0 was a top_k mismatch. Re-running the baseline caught it; it's written up in BUGS.md

name: ShelfSense
description: A shop's Ring camera keeps the bill: it sees what leaves each shelf, names it from the shop's own photos, tracks stock, and leaves anything unsure for a person to check at the exit. Product naming is 98.4% correct within a shelf of 5 products; finding takes on handheld clips is still weak (2 of 8). Built solo for the Amazon Developer Hackathon (Ring track).

deepdive.tagline: A shop's Ring camera keeps the bill, and leaves anything unsure for a person to check at the exit.
deepdive.overview: When a hand goes into a shelf zone empty and comes out holding something, that's a take, and the product is named by matching the hand crop against the shop's own photos. Put-backs flag the matching line. Uncertain lines are marked verify at exit; the system only adds or flags lines, only a person removes one, and every decision is logged. Shoppers watch their bill live from a per-session link, and between visits the camera reads how full each shelf is for restock alerts.
deepdive.why: Small shops already have a camera. The goal was billing and stock from that camera without ever guessing with someone's money.

components.name: Funnel
components.description: The cheap model on every frame (13-15 ms), one batched yes/no VLM question per shelf visit (~200 ms), and catalogue matching only on a take (49 ms), using only the products on that shelf.

components.name: vjev
components.description: Turns VLM answers into typed, calibrated decisions. Boxes reach 86.3% Acc@0.5 on RefCOCO, and it abstains on 93.8% of absent targets.

components.name: Ring integration
components.description: Device list, live view over WHEP pulled server-side (0.6-0.9 s setup, 1280x720 at 29 fps, about 10 fps analysed), the 30 s / 60 s live-view cap, HMAC-signed motion webhooks and account linking, tested on the Ring Developer Portal Playground.

components.name: Exit check and shopper view
components.description: Staff see each flagged line's evidence and keep or remove it with a note; shoppers can tap Not mine.

metrics: Naming: 98.4% within a shelf of 5 products (81 products, 500 queries); 70% on CCTV-quality crops
Shelf watch: AUROC 0.88 on 484 shelf crops; 82.2% on held-out shelves, catching 92% of empty gaps
Ring: 3 of 3 live WHEP sessions connected and analysed
Not there yet: 2 of 8 takes found on handheld clips (1 false)

name: TillLess
description: Queue-free billing from the CCTV a store already has. It spots which shelf slot a shopper's hand takes from, maps the slot to a product, and has the bill ready by the exit; shoppers only scan what it's unsure about. The interaction detector hits 0.80 frame mAP on MERL Shopping, and training on degraded video cut accuracy loss on a bad camera from 0.27 to 0.07 mAP.

deepdive.tagline: Queue-free billing using the CCTV a store already has.
deepdive.overview: TillLess watches which shelf slot each shopper's hand takes from, and the store's shelf map (planogram) turns that slot into a product. By the time the trolley reaches the exit, the bill is ready. Shoppers only scan items the system isn't sure about, and anything disputed goes to staff for a check, never automatic removal. It's software only, with no new cameras. It was the CCTV research groundwork for ShelfSense.
deepdive.why: Checkout queues at Indian supermarkets come down to one thing: billing happens at the end. Amazon's Just Walk Out needs a store rebuilt around it. Most Indian stores already have CCTV, so I started there. The same camera layer can later handle stock alerts, loss prevention and live online inventory.

components.name: Interaction detector
components.description: Frozen ResNet-18 features feed a dilated temporal CNN with a boundary head, so it catches when a hand takes from a shelf and when. 0.80 frame mAP on the MERL Shopping benchmark, with timing within ±0.5 s.

components.name: CCTV robustness
components.description: I swept bitrate, frame rate and resolution. Dropping to 8 fps costs almost nothing; resolution is what hurts. Training on degraded video cut the accuracy loss on a poor camera (230×170, 6 fps, 80 kbps) from 0.27 to 0.07 mAP.

components.name: Throughput
components.description: About 14 real-time camera streams per T4, with a path to cheap in-store edge boxes.

components.name: Market work
components.description: Teardowns of Just Walk Out, Zippin, Grabango (which shut down) and Wobot, Indian retail economics, and DPDP Act compliance.

metrics: 0.80 frame mAP on MERL Shopping, timing within ±0.5 s
Poor-camera accuracy loss cut from 0.27 to 0.07 mAP
~14 real-time streams per T4 GPU
Next: slot-level localisation on RetailAction, then real store pilots

name: clipy
description: Record yourself using a web app, and clipy works out which values flow between its API requests, which requests actually matter, and writes a Python script that replays the flow. One recording went from 25 requests to the 5 it needed. Built overnight, 33 tests, CI on Linux, macOS and Windows.

deepdive.tagline: Turns a browser session into a replay script that pulls fresh tokens from live responses.
deepdive.overview: clipy drives Chrome over the raw DevTools Protocol, records every request, then works out the data dependencies between them. You get a runnable Python script, a Mermaid diagram of the flow and a short report. It's the open-source version of Invariant's session-replay scan.
deepdive.why: At Attack Capital I automated integrations by replaying internal API calls instead of scraping the UI, and it cut the work from weeks to hours. I did the dependency tracing by hand every time. clipy is the tool I wanted back then.

components.name: Recorder
components.description: Drives Chrome, Edge or Brave and follows new tabs, iframes and workers. It reads raw CDP events instead of a typed crate, so a new Chrome release can't break it.

components.name: Dependency analysis
components.description: Links a value in one response to the request that later uses it. The evidence bar scales with how random the value looks, so short ids and common words don't create fake links, and a response only counts if it finished before the request started.

components.name: Code generation
components.description: The replay reads tokens from live responses. CI checks out against a freshly restarted demo shop where every recorded token is already dead.

components.name: Secrets vault
components.description: Recordings are safe to commit. Secrets are sealed with a key that never touches the file, and --forget destroys the key.

metrics: 25 recorded requests reduced to the 5 that mattered
33 tests, CI on Linux, macOS and Windows
About 5.9k lines of Rust, built in one night
Deterministic: no LLM anywhere in the pipeline

name: QuantEdge
description: A quant research platform in Rust that I run every day. It picks stocks from momentum, fundamentals, insider filings and macro signals, backtests with a real cost model, and logs each day's picks to a hash-chained file before their outcomes are known, so I can't quietly tune results after the fact.

deepdive.tagline: Built around one rule: the only evidence that counts is a prediction written down before you know if it was right.
deepdive.overview: QuantEdge has a point-in-time data layer, a multi-factor stock picker, a backtester and a forward-test log nobody can edit without it showing. Most of the effort went into making look-ahead bias impossible by construction.
deepdive.why: Backtests always look good if you're allowed to fit them to the past. I wanted a setup where I couldn't fool myself, even if I tried.

components.name: Signals
components.description: Momentum, fundamentals z-scored within GICS sector (keyed to the actual SEC filing date), insider buying from Form 4, and macro. I tested GDELT and Reddit sentiment live and switched them off because they didn't hold up.

components.name: Natural-language strategies
components.description: Write a strategy in plain English, like 'weight momentum 2x, ignore insiders for tech', and it becomes signal weights.

components.name: Backtester
components.description: Next-open fills, spread, slippage and square-root market impact, rank-IC checks, a drawdown circuit breaker, and VaR/CVaR reporting. The data layer can't return anything dated after the as-of date; SQL enforces it and Rust checks again.

components.name: Forward-test log
components.description: CI logs the model's picks every trading day. Each entry carries the hash of the previous one, so editing or deleting history breaks the chain.

metrics: 194 Rust tests, clippy in CI
NSE and US markets (live universe: 318 US stocks)
Point-in-time fundamentals and S&P 500 membership
Picks logged daily by CI into a hash chain

name: Recourse
description: Helps a California tenant file a small-claims petition to get a security deposit back. It interviews you in plain language, checks eligibility and fees against dated statute text, fills the official SC-100 form, and hands you a report showing where every claim came from. Built in about 39 hours for LexHack 2026.

deepdive.tagline: Legal paperwork where the model is never the one deciding the law.
deepdive.overview: Recourse walks a self-represented tenant from a messy description of what happened to a filled SC-100 and a grounding report. Thresholds and fees are computed in code against dated statute excerpts. The model only extracts facts, checks them and parses sources you paste in.
deepdive.why: Deposit disputes are simple on paper and miserable to file alone. A tool that hallucinates a filing fee is worse than no tool, so I kept the law in code and used the model only where it's actually good.

components.name: Intake and pre-screen
components.description: Plain-language intake. Evictions, lockouts and safety issues get routed to the court's self-help center or legal aid instead, with an override.

components.name: Rule checks
components.description: Eligibility and filing-fee tiers computed against statute text with dates, not asked of the model.

components.name: Self-verification
components.description: The schema asks for evidence before the verdict, because structured output is generated in order and verdict-first let the model rationalize. A deterministic check overrides a 'supported' verdict when its own note contradicts it.

components.name: Form filling
components.description: Fills the official SC-100 and generates a separate grounding report. Names are matched back to the source text after the model swapped one accented character.

metrics: 20 tests: name matching, fee tiers, PDF text, contradiction checks
Built in about 39 hours
Live: recourse-pearl.vercel.app

name: forge
description: Version control for AI agent prompts. Every edit gets a commit with a word-level diff, rollback and forks. Before you commit, it writes a realistic test message and runs the old and new prompt on it, so you see how the behavior changes before you keep the edit. 78 tests, built in about 26 hours. Won the AI Innovation Excellence Award at the AI Builders Hackathon (one of 7 awards, 500+ projects).

deepdive.tagline: Git for agent prompts, where the diff that matters is the behavior.
deepdive.overview: forge gives each agent's system prompt a real history: commits, word-level diffs, one-click rollback and forks. The interesting part is the behavioral diff, which runs the same message through two versions and compares the outputs.
deepdive.why: Prompt changes break agents silently. A text diff tells you what you changed; it doesn't tell you what the agent will now do. I wanted that answer before committing.

components.name: Prompt history
components.description: Commits, word-level diffs, rollback and forks for every agent.

components.name: Behavioral diff
components.description: An LLM writes a realistic test message from the prompt, both versions answer it, and you compare the outputs side by side.

components.name: Regression checks
components.description: Exact-match tests kept flagging harmless paraphrases, so I switched to a temperature-0 judge with a deterministic fallback when the judge's output is malformed.

components.name: Storage
components.description: Moving from localStorage to Postgres surfaced real multi-writer races. I replaced a delete-and-recreate save with per-agent upserts and handled concurrent first-visit seeding. API keys stay in the browser on purpose, so a database leak can't expose them.

metrics: AI Innovation Excellence Award, AI Builders Hackathon 2026 (1 of 7 awards, 500+ projects)
78 tests across 15 files
Built in about 26 hours
Live: forge-theta-two.vercel.app

name: VaultScope
description: IPsec VPN analyzer for Smart India Hackathon 2026 (NTRO problem statement). I built most of the analysis core: the IKEv1/v2 parser that rebuilds each session's crypto negotiation, the ingestion and flow-feature stages, both classifiers, and part of the CVE-linked rules engine. The traffic classifier, which guesses what's running inside an encrypted tunnel, went from 0.79 to 0.98 macro-F1 on the team's dataset.

name: WTP Dynamic Pricing
description: Checkout pricing that adapts to willingness to pay, sitting between a merchant's checkout and Razorpay. It decides price and offer in under 200 ms, explains each decision with SHAP, and never charges a low-trust buyer more than list price. LightGBM regressor R² ≈ 0.91, conversion classifier AUC ≈ 0.72. Razorpay Buildathon 2026, Track 01.

name: Amazon ML Challenge
description: Entity resolution for Amazon ML Challenge 2026: match messy business records from two sources to a clean reference set, with no external data and models under 8B parameters. A fine-tuned mBERT bi-encoder retrieves candidates through FAISS and a DistilBERT cross-encoder re-ranks them. I led a team of three over a three-day sprint. Final leaderboard: 0.961 macro F0.5.

name: Document Pile System
description: A hiring assignment for an AI document company. It takes a pile of related contracts, extracts facts that must appear near-verbatim in the source, flags conflicts between documents, and puts every change behind a human approval step. People use a review UI and agents drive it over MCP. Extraction scored P 0.845 / R 0.740 on 18 CUAD contracts.

name: Tool Dependency Graph
description: A hiring assignment for an agent-tooling company. It reads a catalog of tool schemas and works out which action produces an id that another action needs, then draws the graph. Every edge comes from the schemas. It ignores parameters like account_id that almost every tool takes, and rejects circular edges where a tool needs the very id it claims to produce.

name: Contract Watchdog
description: An agent that watches a small business's contracts and only pulls in a human for a real decision, like a renewal inside its notice window or a price jump. In a live test the model re-notified on a contract it had just flagged and made up a reason, so I moved the dedup check into the tool's code with a regression test. It drafts emails but can't send them. 14 tests.

name: Cash Flow Oracle
description: Settlement forecasting for merchants, 30 to 60 days out with confidence intervals. GARCH(1,1) handles volatility, an HMM spots regime shifts, and Prophet does the trend. It also flags stress periods and suggests credit before a crunch. Razorpay Buildathon 2026, Track 04.

name: PACER
description: Can epoch-based memory reclamation for lock-free data structures adapt to workload pressure? I built it in C++ and Rust and benchmarked it against token4 (PPoPP '24). My early 10–22% speedup turned out to be a use-after-free in my own code. After the fix it ties the baseline, and the repo shows exactly how I found out.

deepdive.tagline: An idea I tested until it either held up or didn't. It didn't, and the write-up says so.
deepdive.overview: PACER asks whether epoch-based reclamation can adapt how aggressively it frees memory based on load. I implemented it twice, as a C++ reclaimer for Brown's setbench and as a Rust core from scratch, then stress-tested both on Linux.
deepdive.why: The first numbers showed a 10–22% win and I didn't believe them. More stress testing found a use-after-free in my reclaimer. A tie with the receipts is worth more than a speedup that crashes 6 runs out of 10.

components.name: C++ reclaimer
components.description: A drop-in reclaimer extending token4. It freed the epoch bag while it was still being written to: heap corruption in 6 of 10 runs at 16 threads. After the fix, 20 of 20 clean runs.

components.name: Rust core
components.description: Tier selection with hysteresis and snapshot coalescing. Tests and the loom model checker caught a livelock and a torn read. Both are fixed and covered by regression tests.

components.name: Backlog tracking
components.description: Watching retired-node backlog, not just throughput, exposed an unbounded leak: 1.5M retired nodes vs 255 for DEBRA. Fixed by splitting per-op and per-window reclamation.

metrics: After the fix: 0.93–1.03× vs token4, a tie
Free-count sweep: K=1 best everywhere; K=64 cost up to 35% throughput
3 concurrency bugs found and fixed, each with a regression test
Raw CSVs behind every number are in the repo

name: Synthetic Market RL
description: A market environment for testing trading agents that simulates prices instead of replaying history, so look-ahead bias can't sneak in. GARCH(1,1) gives volatility clustering, an HMM switches regimes, and Poisson-timed news shocks move correlated assets together. Three difficulty tiers, served over FastAPI in Docker.

deepdive.tagline: A trading environment that generates the market instead of replaying it, so the agent can't peek at the future.
deepdive.overview: Most backtesting environments replay historical data, which leaks the future in ways that are easy to miss. This one simulates market dynamics from statistical properties, so the agent only ever sees what has happened so far.
deepdive.why: I kept seeing agents look brilliant on replayed data and fall apart live. Simulation doesn't fix every problem, but it removes the one that bit me most.

components.name: Market engine
components.description: GARCH(1,1) volatility clustering plus hidden-Markov regime switching: volatility clusters, trends and mean reversion.

components.name: Difficulty tiers
components.description: Tier 1 is single-asset trend following. Tier 2 is two assets with guaranteed regime switches. Tier 3 is a four-asset portfolio under stress with a hard drawdown stop.

components.name: News shocks
components.description: 50+ headline templates arrive at Poisson-timed intervals, with Cholesky sampling so correlated assets move together.

components.name: Deployment
components.description: A REST server in Docker with a validation suite for every tier.

metrics: GARCH(1,1) + HMM regime switching
3 difficulty tiers
50+ news templates on Poisson timing
Correlated multi-asset moves via Cholesky sampling

name: MoE on a 4 GB GPU
description: Mixture-of-experts models like OLMoE-1B-7B need about 14 GB of GPU memory. I measured what happens when only about 20% of the experts fit, on two models and a real 4 GB laptop GPU. The best setup keeps fp16 experts resident and serves misses from int4 copies: 0.24x the memory, HellaSwag 77.2 vs 77.4, and 2.2x faster than standard offloading.

deepdive.tagline: What it actually takes to run a mixture-of-experts LLM on a laptop GPU.
deepdive.overview: OLMoE-1B-7B and IBM's Granite MoE need far more memory than a typical laptop GPU has. I studied keeping only a fraction of the experts resident, across five pre-registered phases on Kaggle GPUs, and checked the results on GSM8K, HellaSwag and ARC-Challenge.
deepdive.why: Most claims about running big models on small hardware come from one benchmark and one model. I wanted numbers I could trust, so every hypothesis was committed to git before its data existed, and the analysis scripts refuse to give a verdict otherwise. The failures are in the report too.

components.name: Cache simulator
components.description: Replays real expert-routing traces under LRU, LFU and the offline-optimal Belady bound, so a caching policy can be judged before touching a GPU.

components.name: Live evaluator
components.description: Rewrites each MoE router's choices in place. Dozens of policies run side by side with the full model in one batch, so quality loss is measured exactly, with a noise floor of zero.

components.name: Mixed-precision fallback
components.description: Resident experts stay fp16; misses are served from int4 copies, plus two refinements found during the study.

metrics: 0.24x GPU memory, HellaSwag 77.2 vs 77.4
2.2x faster than standard offloading
Exact offloading is too slow at this budget, even under the Belady bound
Skipping missing experts breaks the model (GSM8K drops to 0%). Replicates on a second architecture

name: SNUXplore
description: The campus app for Shiv Nadar University. I led all the tech as one of three project leads on a team of about 23 (most of the team ran marketing and on-ground work), and I'm the largest code contributor. 30,000+ uses in its first week. A RAG layer answers questions about courses, professors and campus. Now on v4.

deepdive.tagline: One campus app instead of five broken ones. 30,000+ uses in its first week.
deepdive.overview: SNUXplore started as a course planner and grew into the place students go for courses, professors, food and campus info. I led all the tech as one of three project leads on a team of about 23, most of whom ran marketing and on-ground work. It's now on v4.
deepdive.why: SNU's tools were scattered and slow. Finding which courses were open, who taught what or what the mess was serving meant asking around. The first week settled whether that was a real problem.

components.name: Spike-ready backend
components.description: Built for registration day, when the whole campus hits the app in the same few minutes.

components.name: RAG answers
components.description: Ask in plain English, like which CS electives a professor teaches, and get an answer pulled from campus documents.

metrics: 30,000+ uses in the first week
Tech lead, one of 3 project leads, ~23-person team
Largest code contributor
Live: snu-xplore-six.vercel.app

name: BuildFlow
description: An AI project manager that remembers your product between sessions. It helps you go from a rough idea to a scoped MVP, writes tasks sized to the team, and tracks them on a Kanban board. We used it at a college event, where it handled 500+ projects.

deepdive.tagline: An AI project manager that doesn't forget your product the moment you close the tab.
deepdive.overview: BuildFlow keeps a persistent picture of your product and helps at each step: rough idea, MVP scope, tasks, tracking. We ran it at a college event, where it handled 500+ projects.
deepdive.why: I was tired of re-explaining my own product to an LLM every session. BuildFlow keeps that context so the AI can actually help with what to build next.

components.name: Ideation with memory
components.description: Remembers the project's history and doesn't suggest things you've already tried.

components.name: MVP scoping
components.description: Separates core features from nice-to-haves and ranks them by impact and effort.

components.name: Task generation
components.description: Tasks sized to the team. A list for a senior engineer looks different from one for a beginner.

metrics: 500+ projects at a college event
Context kept across sessions
Task generation + Kanban tracking

name: Locus
description: A multiplayer canvas where people and an AI agent think together. The AI gets its own cursor, draws nodes and talks. The canvas is a typed JSON op log in Aurora DSQL streamed over SSE, so the agent reads structure instead of pixels. Built in about five days for the H0 hackathon run by Vercel and AWS.

name: loom-boom-zoom
description: A Loom-style studio for demo videos that runs entirely in your browser: script, teleprompter, recording, compositing and export. Whisper transcribes locally and ffmpeg.wasm renders, so you don't need an account and your footage never leaves your machine.

name: ChainedThought
description: A multi-agent research system I built in November 2024, a few months before the big deep-research products shipped. It splits a hard question into domain questions, sends each to a specialist agent, and an orchestrator merges the answers while keeping track of where the agents disagree.

deepdive.tagline: Specialist agents argue a question from different angles, and the orchestrator keeps the disagreements.
deepdive.overview: ChainedThought takes a complex question, breaks it into domain questions, and hands each to a specialist agent: economics, funding, technology, regulation and so on. An orchestrator writes the final answer and lists where the specialists agreed, where they contradicted each other, and what nobody covered.
deepdive.why: A single agent answers from one angle and misses the rest. I wanted the disagreements in the open, because that's usually where the interesting part of a question is.

components.name: Question decomposition
components.description: Splits the query into domain questions and spins up one agent per domain.

components.name: Specialist agents
components.description: Each has its own priors, tools and criteria. They're supposed to disagree.

components.name: Orchestrator
components.description: Merges the answers and tracks agreements, contradictions and gaps.

metrics: Built November 2024
One specialist agent per domain
Contradictions tracked explicitly in the final answer

name: NewsOCR / BookOCR
description: Tesseract pulls the text and a local LLM cleans it up and structures it. Cheaper than cloud OCR, and it holds up on real books and newspapers. The same OCR core later went into the Pactle quote engine for scanned RFQs.

name: OS Resource Manager
description: A simulated OS resource manager: scheduling that learns from usage patterns, predictive memory allocation, and process trust scoring for anomaly detection, tested on 100–200 simulated processes. Written up as an IEEE-style paper.

name: AdvisoryAI
description: A .NET engine for Word templates. It treats highlighted sections as blanks and fills them from an LLM or structured input, so a template works without anyone hand-editing it. Built at a hackathon.

name: Petner
description: My first startup, started at 18: a social platform for pet owners. I rebuilt it four times in a year (petnerSocial, v1, Next, Plat) before shutting it down. It taught me more about distribution than any course.

name: DeBi
description: An NFT launchpad that let a business issue its own fungible or non-fungible tokens, pitched as a digital IPO. Solidity contracts with a React front end, built in 2023.

name: DeLogi
description: QR-based supply chain provenance: every scan at a production or logistics step adds to an audit trail for the product. Co-built as part of CatalystIQ. We shut it down because the Indian market wasn't ready for it.

name: Crypto Tx Tracker
description: Paste a transaction and it follows the money to whatever depth you set, so you can see whether funds from a flagged transaction were later withdrawn or mixed. Built in 2023, before this was a standard compliance feature.

name: News Bias Analyzer
description: Summarizes a news article, classifies its political lean, then searches for coverage of the same story from the other side and flags when it finds contradicting reports.
